title: Booking & empty release
sceneDesc: A booking request travels from the shipper to the carrier and a confirmation comes back. In an empty-container depot, a truck drives in, an empty container is lowered onto it, inspected at the gate and driven out.

narration.1: The [[shipper]] reserves space for me on a ship, from {pol} to {pod}: that's the [[booking]].
narration.2: It starts with a [[booking]] request: equipment type and quantity, {pol} → {pod}, commodity ({cargo}), estimated weight, preferred sailing and the contract or quote behind the rate. [TO VERIFY:v30]
narration.3: Booking request via portal, platform or EDI against a service contract or spot quote. Special cargo — reefer, DG, OOG — needs approval before confirmation. [TO VERIFY:v30]

caption.2: Under {incoterm}, the {freightBy} side contracts the ocean freight with the carrier.

narration.1: The carrier confirms space and an empty box with a [[booking-confirmation]]: my travel plan.
narration.2: Customer service validates allocation, equipment and approvals, then issues the [[booking-confirmation]]. Open it: every line drives a later step.
narration.3: Confirmation against allocation and equipment availability. Watch the fine print: cut-offs, free time, pick-up and return locations, special-cargo approvals.

caption.2: Carriers may accept slightly more bookings than slots to offset no-shows. [TO VERIFY:v31]

narration.1: A truck collects me, empty, at the [[depot]].
narration.2: The haulier presents the [[release-order|release reference]]. [[equipment-control|Equipment control]] allocated the type and, if needed, a grade (food quality, {family}).
narration.3: Empty release against the reference; grade and condition must match the commodity. Reefers need a passed [[pti]], tanks a cleanliness check, OOG equipment the right fittings. [TO VERIFY:v57]

2.reefer: Reefer: [[pti]] passed, [[set-point]] {setPoint} programmed before release. [TO VERIFY:v56]
2.tank: Tank: last cargo and cleaning checked — tanks are usually supplied by tank operators. [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.oog: Special equipment is scarce: the depot may need time to supply it. [TO VERIFY:v58]
2.*: Wrong box for the cargo (dirty, damaged) = refused at stuffing and a second truck trip.

narration.1: At the gate, my condition is noted on an [[eir]] and my [[detention]] clock starts.
narration.2: Gate-out inspection recorded on the [[eir]], often digital with photos. The export [[detention]] clock runs until full gate-in at the terminal. [TO VERIFY:v21]
narration.3: EIR at gate-out, movement reported to the carrier (EDI CODECO). Export detention clock starts per tariff. [TO VERIFY:v36] [TO VERIFY:v21]

Two days before the cut-off, capacity management cuts the allocation on {vessel}: your customer's box is on the list of bookings to roll to next week's sailing. The customer's letter of credit requires shipment by this week.

text.1: Asia ships more to Europe than it buys back, so many boxes return empty. [TO VERIFY:v38]
text.2: Empties are about 20% of all container handling in ports. [TO VERIFY:v38]

body.1: The exporter or its forwarder makes the booking. Under {incoterm}, the ocean freight is arranged by the {freightBy}; when that's the buyer, its forwarder near {pol} usually books for it.
body.2: The booking party is not always the B/L shipper. A forwarder acting as [[nvocc]] books in its own name and issues its own house B/L. [TO VERIFY:v34]

body.1: The carrier's customer service checks space and equipment, then confirms. Many bookings are made online.
body.2: Checks: allocation by trade and customer, equipment at the depot, rate validity, special approvals (DG desk, reefer, OOG). [TO VERIFY:v30]

body.1: The price of the trip: ocean freight plus surcharges such as [[baf]] (fuel) and port handling ([[thc]]).
body.2: All-in, or base rate + surcharges (BAF, peak season, origin/destination THC, documentation fee). Names and structures vary by carrier. [TO VERIFY:v35]

body.1: A yard where empty containers wait between trips. They are inspected, cleaned and repaired there.
body.2: Often run by a third party under contract: storage, maintenance and repair ([[mnr]]), cleaning, reefer PTI. Gate movements are reported electronically. [TO VERIFY:v36]

body.1: A forklift-like machine built to lift and stack light, empty containers.
body.2: Designed for empty boxes only; full boxes need reach stackers or yard cranes. [TO VERIFY:v37]

reefer.1: Before a reefer leaves the depot, its cooling machine is tested ([[pti]]) and set to the temperature the shipper asked for: {setPoint} for {cargo}.
reefer.2: PTI passed and [[set-point]] {setPoint} programmed; ventilation and humidity settings per booking. A wrong set point is a classic cause of cargo claims. [TO VERIFY:v56] [TO VERIFY:v57]

tank.1: Tanks carry liquids, often dangerous. The tank must be clean and suitable for {cargo}.
tank.2: Tank containers are usually supplied by tank operators; the last cargo and cleaning certificate must be compatible with the new product. DG approval is required at booking. [TO VERIFY:v59]

oog.1: {box} boxes are rarer than standard ones, so they must be ordered early.
oog.2: OOG bookings need the exact dimensions and weight, and approval by the special-cargo desk and vessel planners before confirmation. [TO VERIFY:v58]

body.1: Equipment Interchange Receipt: a short report on my condition each time I change hands — dents, holes, cleanliness.
body.2: Signed or digitally confirmed by driver and depot, often with photos. Damage found later without an EIR record can be charged to the merchant.

body.1: The container belongs to the carrier. After the free days, every extra day outside costs money: that's [[detention]].
body.2: Export detention typically runs from empty gate-out to full gate-in (merchant haulage). Illustrative free time: {freeDays} days, then {cur}80 per day. [TO VERIFY:v21] [TO VERIFY:v12]
body.3: Collect the empty too early and free time burns before the cut-off. Some carriers combine demurrage and detention into one free-time pool. [TO VERIFY:v21]

1.2: Size-type code per ISO 6346 ({boxCode}). Substituting equipment needs the customer's agreement. [TO VERIFY:v32]
1.3: Equipment and commodity drive approvals: a change of commodity after confirmation (e.g. to DG) requires a new approval.

2.2: Documentation (SI), VGM and port (CY) cut-offs. Order and timing vary by carrier and port. [TO VERIFY:v20]

3.2: From the tariff or the customer's contract. Illustrative value from CONFIG. [TO VERIFY:v12]

2.prompt: Which deadline comes first in this booking?

options.fb: The full box can arrive last; paperwork closes earlier.
Here the VGM closes after the SI.

2.explain: Here the SI closes first, then the VGM, then the port cut-off. Sequences vary by carrier and port — always read the confirmation. [TO VERIFY:v20]

3.prompt: Empty picked up Day 1, full gate-in at {polTerminal} Day 5, free time {freeDays} days (export detention). What is billed?

options.text: Nothing — the box was back within the free time
4 days of detention, counted from Day 1 to Day 5
options.fb: Days are charged only beyond the free time.

options.text: 5 days of demurrage at the export terminal yard
options.fb: Demurrage covers time inside the terminal, not this period.

options.text: It depends on the Incoterm agreed in the sale contract
options.fb: Billing follows the tariff or contract; the Incoterm only shapes who should bear it between seller and buyer.

3.explain: Detention runs gate-out to gate-in per tariff; 4 days < {freeDays} free days. Who ultimately bears D&D between seller and buyer is a sales-contract question. [TO VERIFY:v21]

documents: **Booking request / confirmation** — portal or EDI (IFTMBF/IFTMBC). [TO VERIFY:v30]
**EIR** at gate-out — the box's condition on record.
**Rate agreement** — service contract or quote reference.
costs: **Ocean freight + surcharges** (BAF, THC…), fixed by contract or quote. [TO VERIFY:v35]
**Cancellation / no-show fees** at some carriers. [TO VERIFY:v31]
**Damage / cleaning recharges** if the return EIR shows new damage.
risks: **Rolled** after overbooking or a [[blank-sailing]]: inform the customer early. [TO VERIFY:v31]
**Wrong equipment grade** → rejected at stuffing, extra trucking.
**Empty collected too early** → free time burnt before the cut-off.

risks.text: **No special approval** for reefer/DG/OOG → booking cannot be confirmed. [TO VERIFY:v58]

jobs: **Capacity / allocation management** — who gets space on which vessel.
**Equipment control** — release, repositioning, depot vendors; **DG / special cargo desk** — approvals.

incoNote.E: The buyer (or its forwarder near {pol}) books and collects the empty.
incoNote.F: The buyer books the freight, so it must pass the booking details to the seller in time.
incoNote.C: The seller books and pays the freight to {pod}.
incoNote.D: The seller books the whole carriage to the buyer's door.

1: Every journey starts with a booking; the booking confirmation sets ship, places and deadlines.
The party paying the ocean freight under the Incoterm makes the booking.
Empty containers come from depots; their condition is recorded on an EIR and the detention clock starts at gate-out.
2: Booking → validation (allocation, equipment, approvals) → confirmation with cut-offs.
Who books follows the Incoterm and the contract of carriage; NVOCCs book in their own name.
Equipment control releases the right type and grade; reefers need PTI and the right set point.
Export detention starts at gate-out, per tariff.
3: Read the confirmation like a contract: cut-off sequence, free time, pick-up/return locations, approvals.
Rollings must be communicated at once — never 'fix' a deadline by misdating a B/L.
Special cargo (reefer, DG, OOG) is approved before confirmation, not after.

1.prompt: I'm an empty container on a truck, just out of the depot. What happens next?
1.hint: I'm empty. Where are the goods waiting?

options.text: The truck takes me to the seller's warehouse, where the goods are put inside me.
options.confirm: Exactly. The goods are waiting at the shipper's premises, so I go there to be filled ('stuffed'). Under {incoterm}, this trip is arranged by {preBy}.

options.text: The truck takes me straight to the port, and I'm loaded onto the ship still empty.
options.why: I'm still empty! The goods are at the shipper's warehouse.
options.realLife: An empty box at the export terminal would be refused, and the shipper would pay for an extra trip.
options.whenRight: Carriers do move empties to ports to reposition them — but that's their own move, not a customer's booking.

options.text: I stay at the depot, and the seller brings the goods here in small vans, one by one.
options.why: Depots only handle empty containers. For a full container load ([[fcl]]), the shipper loads its own goods.
options.realLife: The depot has no goods and no staff to load them: the truck would wait for nothing.
options.whenRight: Small shipments ([[lcl]]) are consolidated at a [[cfs]] — a different service and place.

2.prompt: Booking confirmed, empty {box} gated out with a clean EIR. What happens next?

options.text: The haulier positions the empty at the shipper's premises for stuffing, within the free time.
options.confirm: Correct. FCL cargo is stuffed at origin by the shipper. Too early burns detention free time; too late puts the VGM and port cut-offs at risk. Under {incoterm}, this leg is for {preBy}.

options.text: The haulier delivers the empty to the export terminal, where the cargo is stuffed before loading.
options.why: Export terminals receive full containers for loading, not empties for stuffing.
options.realLife: Refused or charged for handling and storage; a second truck move puts the cut-offs at risk.
options.whenRight: For [[lcl]] or port-side services, cargo is stuffed at a [[cfs]] near the port — another booking and service.

options.text: The shipper submits the SI and asks the carrier to issue the original B/L against the booking.
options.why: A B/L needs actual cargo details (seal, packages, weights) and the carrier must have taken charge of the goods — the box is still empty.
options.realLife: A B/L issued before receiving the goods certifies something untrue: fraud exposure and L/C problems.
options.whenRight: Early SI submission is fine once data is final; the B/L comes after receipt or loading.

options.text: The depot weighs the empty container so that the shipper can declare the VGM to the carrier.
options.why: The [[tare]] is marked on the door and the [[csc-plate]]. The VGM is the packed container's weight — after stuffing.
options.realLife: A 'VGM' declared before stuffing is not verified: misdeclaration and unsafe stowage. [TO VERIFY:v02]
options.whenRight: Method 2 uses the marked tare plus weighed contents — no depot weighing needed.

3.prompt: Case: allocation is cut and the booking is on the roll list. The customer's L/C requires shipment this week. What should you do first?

options.text: Tell the customer now and offer options: another service this week, or time to amend the L/C.
options.confirm: Right. Early, documented communication with alternatives is the professional standard; the shipper can then act with its bank. Never adjust a B/L date to fit the L/C. [TO VERIFY:v31]

options.text: Keep the booking quietly and issue the B/L with this week's vessel and date, as the L/C requires.
options.why: A B/L must reflect the vessel and date the goods were actually shipped on.
options.realLife: Misdated or false B/Ls are fraud: the carrier loses its defences and may face L/C fraud claims.

options.text: Wait for the final load list before telling the customer, to avoid worrying them for nothing.
options.why: Waiting removes the customer's options (other service, L/C amendment).
options.realLife: The customer discovers the rolling at the last minute: missed L/C, penalties, lost account.
options.whenRight: Only if the roll list is still provisional — and even then, a heads-up is better.

options.text: Cancel the booking, refund the customer and suggest they look for space with another carrier.
options.why: Cancelling doesn't ship the goods; the customer needs a solution, not a refund.
options.realLife: The customer must rebook at a possibly higher spot rate and still misses the L/C date.
options.whenRight: If the customer chooses to cancel after being offered alternatives.
